messages.subject: Ordinal regression intercept sign
parts:
Hi all,
I am new to the brms package and I'm after some clarification with regards to the intercepts behaviour in an ordinal regression model.

This is my model (btw, do these priors make sense? Only looking for something weakly informative. To be honest, I am more familiar to the rstanarm package...).
 
mod_brms <- brm(MyDV | weights(DEMWGT)  ~ OSATB_FULL + OSATD_FULL + OSATG_FULL + (1 + OSATB_FULL + OSATD_FULL + OSATG_FULL | ID),

                  data=prepaid_j1w, family=cumulative,

                  prior = c(set_prior("normal(0,3)", class="Intercept"), set_prior("normal(0,3)", class="b"), set_prior("cauchy(0,2)", class="sd"), set_prior("lkj(2)", class = "cor")),

                  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99))



This is the output:

My concern is around those intercepts. When I extract the model coefficients, the predictors coefficients are indeed the sum of the population-level effects and the corresponding group-level effects. But for the intercepts what I am getting is that the overall model intercepts are ranef(intercept) minus fixef(intercept). Why is that so?


Thanks,
Paul

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Ordinal regression intercept sign
parts:
Hi Paul,

in the usual definition of the cumulative family, the probability for category k is given by

F(Intercept[k+1] - eta) - F(Intercept[k] - eta)

where F is a cumulative distribution function (the logistic distribution using the logit link),
and eta contain all fixed and random effects predictor terms except for the fixed effects intercepts (also called thresholds in ordinal models).

This formulation ensures that positive regression coefficients imply higher prob. for higher categories when the value of the predictor is larger.

Howver, in this notation, we have to compute fixed - random effects intercepts to get to the intercepts for each group, since the random intercepts
are part or eta.

With respect to the priors: Yes they seem ok, although I would except the model to run well without specifying them.

One question though: For what reason did you add weights to your model?

messages.author: 50376cb8eda8eca6
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Ordinal regression intercept sign
parts:
Hi Paul,

Thank you for taking the time to explain this to me. Would I be correct in assuming that, by extension, this parameterisation is similar to what SPSS and the R packages MASS and ordinal use, so that - as you mention in your reply - bigger and positive coefficients imply higher probabilities for higher categories?

Using the priors actually helped the model - before introducing them, I was having problems both with divergent transitions and most often with large tree-depths. 
To answer your question about the weights, I should add that I work in marketing research where weighting our survey data is - unfortunately - the name of the game. Indeed I am never comfortable with using weights when modelling, mostly because it seems to me that there is not much literature about it (by the way, if there is any good paper that you could suggest around weighting and modelling that would be great!). Basically those weights are there so that my colleagues are happy that I have actually used them! I suppose this is one of the many compromises you have to make when working in an environment like mine!

This actually brings to my next question. Because of my line of work, I'd be interested in using this model to build a quick and dirty simulator - something that a client could use (most likely in Excel) to see the effect on the DV by simply changing one the IVs. Would it be possible? Alternately, can I predict the probabilities for an average ID, similarly to what's been done in pages 6 and 7 of this vignette for the ordinal package? 


Thanks again,
Paul

messages.author: 6e3dd74b422c061b
messages.subject: Re: [brms-users] Ordinal regression intercept sign
parts:
Yes you are correct in assuming that.

Consider using the predict or fitted method with argument re_formula = NA (to exclude all random effects and just take the mean effect) and pass your desired IV combinations via argument newdata.

Best,
Paul
